_comment: Branch protection for `main`, as a file.
It lived in the repository settings, which is a page: a change there leaves
no diff, no review, no history and nobody to notice. CODEOWNERS already
says who owns what, but nothing said that a pull request is required at
all, which checks must be green, or whether `main` can be force-pushed — so
'is this branch protected' could only be answered by opening the settings,
and 'was it protected last month' could not be answered at all.
HOW TO APPLY IT. GitHub does not read `.github/rulesets/`; being here
protects nothing. Import it once:
Settings -> Rules -> Rulesets -> New ruleset -> Import a ruleset
or:  gh api repos/stackvo/stackvo/rulesets --method POST --input .github/rulesets/main.json
From then on this file is what gets reviewed and the page is what gets
checked against it. Change both in the same pull request — a drift between
them is the invisible state this was written to replace.
WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT HERE, because a rule that cannot be satisfied is a
rule that gets bypassed until it is switched off:
* `required_approving_review_count` is 0, not 1. This repository has one
contributor. Requiring an approval would mean every pull request waits
for a second person who does not exist, and the honest end of that is
an admin merging past the rule every time. The gate that does work here
is the checks below: a pull request is still required, and it still has
to be green. Raise this to 1 the day there is a second maintainer.
* `required_linear_history` is absent. Half this history is merge commits
(35 of 72) because pull requests are merged, not rebased. Turning it on
would not tidy the past, it would reject the way the project actually
works — and if that way should change, changing it is the decision, not
this file.
* `required_signatures` is absent. Local commits here are unsigned today;
GitHub signs its own merge commits, which is why `git log --show-signature`
looks half-signed. Requiring signatures before setting up a signing key
would lock the only maintainer out of their own repository. It is a
worthwhile thing to turn on, and the order is: set up the key, verify a
commit shows Verified, then add the rule here.
`required_status_checks` names CI JOB NAMES, not workflows — the `name:`
fields in `ci.yml`, plus the two scanning jobs and the dependency review.
The three OS rows come from the matrix, so renaming a job or dropping a
matrix entry silently stops requiring it. That is the price of naming checks
at all, and it is a smaller price than requiring none.
name: main
